---
title: "Wild Cats at the Urban Edge"
subtitle: "Pumas and bobcats in San Francisco Bay Area open spaces"
author: "Kiran Balasubramanian"
date: last-modified
---

Two wild cats share the same ecosystem in the San Francisco Bay Area, and they present opposite analysis challenges.
Bobcats are common and occurrence data are plenty. Pumas are rare, wide-ranging, and their
precise locations are a risk to publish. One landscape has two data situations that
point in different directions. This project analyses them separately.

## What is studied?

[`Identifying Conservation Success Stories`](https://k-bsub.github.io/tiger-conservation-india/) studied
tiger recovery in select reserves in India. That study had a national census: five repeated survey 
rounds that made "population change over time" the question to ask.

The Bay Area has no equivalent for either species. There is one recent statewide
mountain lion abundance estimate and no statewide bobcat estimate at all. 

What the region does have is dense, well-kept open-source data on land protection, road
mortality, and landscape structure. This project studies **distribution and coexistence 
at the urban–wildland edge** — where the
animals are, how they move, and where their movement meets the roads.

## Ten counties, roughly eight million people

The study area is the ten-county San Francisco Bay Area: Alameda, Contra Costa,
Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Santa Cruz, Solano, and
Sonoma. Roughly eight million people live inside this frame, next to a patchwork
of parks, watershed lands, ranch easements, and open-space preserves.

Pumas and bobcats persist here at the urban edge. The relevant questions are about movement, 
permeability, and coexistence.

## Two species, two analysis

The two species are analysed in parallel and never aggregated.

| | Puma | Bobcat |
|---|---|---|
| Occurrence records | Sparse | Abundant |
| Location sensitivity | High — coarsened on publish | Low |
| Home range | Very large (100s of km²) | Small (10s of km²) |
| Primary story | Isolation and connectivity | Occupancy and distribution |
| Primary method | Least-cost paths and corridors | Occupancy models, KDE, Gi\* |

The puma data has 1,028 precise, publicly shared occurrence points inside the
study frame. That number is small for an animal that ranges over hundreds of
square kilometres, so the puma work is built around connectivity: where the core
habitat patches are, and how an animal could move between them. The precise
points are never published — every puma map is generalised first.

The bobcat track is the opposite. Records are abundant, so the work is about
distribution: which open-space units bobcats occupy, and which landscape
characteristics best explain that pattern.

## Five questions

The analysis is organised around five questions:

1. **Landscape.** How is protected open space distributed across the ten counties,
   and how connected or fragmented is it from the view of a wide-ranging carnivore?
2. **Bobcat.** Where are bobcats present across open-space units, and which
   landscape characteristics best explain that pattern?
3. **Puma.** Where are the likely movement corridors between core habitat patches,
   and where do those corridors cross major roads and high-traffic barriers?
4. **Both.** Where do the modeled puma corridors cross major roads and
   high-traffic barriers, and where is wildlife–vehicle collision risk therefore
   concentrated? Direct mortality records are pending; the road crossings serve
   as the interim risk proxy.
5. **Cross-cutting.** How much of the apparent spatial pattern reflects true
   distribution, and how much reflects observer and detection effort?

The fifth question is treated as a result. Detection
effort shapes every descriptive layer in the project, and the two species answer
it in opposite ways: the bobcat occupancy model corrects for effort, while the puma
corridors do not depend on it.
